330.title: What year one gave
330.hook: the prophets, the Prophet ﷺ, the prayer, the juz', the names, the book
330.howItsDone: There is no single custom for the end of a year of learning; Muslim teachers and students often review what was learned before starting something new, and some close a course of study with du'a.

segments.voice: Yesterday, heard in the world, rabb al-'alamin: from Jakarta to Dakar, the same Arabic. Your line was the same words everywhere.

A year is too big to remember all at once. It comes back in pieces: a word, a story, a habit that stuck, a line you can say without looking. This path has handed you pieces like that for three hundred and twenty-nine days, starting with one word at the door: salaam. Tomorrow is the lookout at the top of year one. Before you stand there, let's gather what the year gave, camp by camp.
screen: `A YEAR COMES BACK IN PIECES.` → `IT STARTED WITH SALAAM.` → `WHAT THE YEAR GAVE.`

segments.voice: Camp one gave you first words. Salaam and bismillah. Alhamdulillah, inshallah. Al-Fatiha, piece by piece: Rabb, rahma, the Day of Judgment, the straight path, amin. Tawhid, the oneness of God at the center of the faith. Wudu, salat, the adhan, Jumu'ah, dhikr, Ramadan, zakat, and the Prophet ﷺ. Camp two gave you the stories. Adam. Nuh and the ark. Ibrahim. Musa and Pharaoh. Yusuf across a whole surah. Maryam and Isa. Yunus in the belly of the fish. Then the Prophet himself: Mecca, the cave, the hijra, the camel kneeling in Medina. Camp three gave you the practices. Salat step by step, dhikr on the fingers, Ramadan and the two Eids, du'a in your own words, the mosque, halal, charity as a habit. Camp four gave you the text: the thirtieth juz', surah by surah, from the short ones at the end back to An-Naba'. Camp five took you further in. The most beautiful names, from Ar-Rahman to As-Sabur. The seerah in Medina, all the way to the farewell sermon and the Prophet's last days. The Sufi path, from Rabi'a to Rumi, ending with dhikr, the heart's polish. And these last three weeks, the book itself: a recitation that, tradition says, arrived over twenty-three years, then was gathered, copied, dotted, translated, explained, recited in many voices, carried by heart and heard all over the world. The Qur'an calls itself, more than once, a reminder. In Pickthall's words: "Lo! We, even We, reveal the Reminder." That's what the year was, underneath all its parts. Not a pile of facts to keep. A year of remembering.
screen: `CAMP ONE: FIRST WORDS` · `CAMPS TWO AND THREE: STORIES, PRACTICES` · `CAMP FOUR: THE THIRTIETH JUZ'` · `CAMP FIVE: FURTHER IN`

segments.voice: On paper or your phone, write five lines, one from each camp: a first word, a story, a practice that stuck if one did, a surah from the juz', and one thing from the depths, a name, a day in Medina, a line from Rumi, something about the book. Don't pick the best; pick the one that stayed.
Tadhkirah. A reminder — what the Qur'an calls itself, and the thread under everything year one gave, camp by camp. Today's word.
Your line: a year of remembering. Five lines can hold a year. Day three hundred thirty, and one day left in year one.

'Lo! We, even We, reveal the Reminder.'

331.title: The big lookout
331.hook: look back down the hill: from salaam on day one to a whole juz' carried in the heart
331.howItsDone: Many Muslims keep a small daily portion of Qur'an reading and remembrance rather than occasional long sessions, following the teaching that the deeds most loved by Allah are the regular ones, even if small.

segments.voice: Yesterday, what year one gave, its tadhkirah: five camps, five lines. Your line was a year of remembering.

Some trails end at a lookout: a wooden rail, a worn bench, a little sign naming the peaks. People who've been staring at their boots for hours stand there and go quiet. Below, you can see the town where you started, small enough to cover with your thumb. Ahead, a further range you didn't know was there. Stand here a minute. This is the last day of camp five, and the last day of year one.
screen: `A WOODEN RAIL, A WORN BENCH.` → `THE TOWN WHERE YOU STARTED.` → `A FURTHER RANGE AHEAD.`

segments.voice: Look back down the hill. Yesterday you gathered the year camp by camp. Up here, you don't need the list; only a few landmarks stand out. Way down at the bottom, one word: salaam, a greeting that is also a wish. Further up, a seven-verse prayer you learned a piece at a time, long before you heard it called the mother of the book. And near the top, a whole juz', thirty-seven surahs, walked backward from An-Nas to An-Naba', carried in the heart, or at least begun there. Notice something else from up here. The path never went straight. It switched back from words to stories, from stories to practice, from practice to the text, then further in. From below, each turn felt like a new subject. From here it looks like one road, circling the same few things: God named and remembered, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ walked beside, a book heard aloud. Now look ahead. Year two is the book, surah by surah: starting from the Opening and al-Baqarah and reading onward, a little each day, all the way to the edge of the juz' you already know. It's a big range. The method doesn't change. The Prophet said, as Bukhari records, that the deeds most loved by Allah are the ones done regularly, even if they're small. That's how this hill was climbed: one small day at a time, from salaam to here.
screen: `LOOK BACK DOWN THE HILL` · `A WHOLE JUZ', BEGUN IN THE HEART` · `ONE ROAD, MANY SWITCHBACKS` · `AHEAD: THE BOOK, SURAH BY SURAH`

segments.voice: Choose the verse that stayed with you most this year, the one you wrote down, a line of al-Fatiha, al-Kawthar, or bismillah itself, and say it once, aloud, slowly, the way you'd speak at the top of a hill. Then stop, rest, and let the whole year lie behind you like a view. If you pray, you can thank Allah in your own words.
Salaam. Peace — the path's very first word, from the same root as Islam and Muslim, seen again from the top of year one. Today's word.
Your line: from here you can see. Tomorrow, year two begins. Day three hundred thirty-one, and year one is yours.

332.title: The whole book
332.hook: a year to read from the Opening to the edge of the juz' you already know
332.tomorrow: Seven verses, said seventeen times a day
332.howItsDone: Many Muslims keep a fixed daily time for reading the Qur'an, often after the dawn prayer, and aim to complete a full reading, a khatm, over a month, a Ramadan, or longer.

segments.voice: Yesterday you stood at the big lookout, at the top of year one, back at salaam. Your line was from here you can see. What did you see when you looked back? Day three hundred thirty-two.

Pick up a printed Qur'an and open it at the front. If it's an Arabic copy, the front is on the right, because Arabic reads right to left. The first page is short: seven verses, often framed in gold. Turn it, and the second surah begins and keeps going for dozens of pages. Year one walked this book from the back, where the surahs are short enough to learn in an afternoon. Year two opens it at the front and reads forward. Today: the whole book.
screen: `OPEN IT AT THE FRONT.` → `SEVEN VERSES, FRAMED IN GOLD.` → `YEAR TWO READS FORWARD.`

segments.voice: The word Qur'an means a recitation, something read aloud. It shares a root with iqra', read, the command that tradition says came to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ in the cave. So the book is named for being heard. The written copy has a different name: mushaf, a bound set of pages. A mushaf is the recitation, bound. Now a fact about the order. The book isn't arranged in the order the verses came down. The verses tradition counts as the first revealed sit near the back, in Surah al-Alaq. The book opens instead with a short prayer and then the long surah al-Baqarah. Scholars hold that the order of verses within each surah was set by the Prophet himself; on the order of the surahs, some say the same, and others say it came partly from his companions. Either way, it's the order Muslims read in today. So this year reads that way. From al-Fatiha, the Opening, through al-Baqarah and the long Medinan surahs, through Yusuf and Maryam and the Cave, onward, until we reach the edge of the part you already walked, the thirtieth juz'. In Ramadan some read one juz' a night and close the book on the last nights. Bukhari records that the Prophet told a companion, Abdullah ibn Amr, who wanted to read it constantly, to take a month for each reading. We'll take a year, a few verses at a time, slow enough to hear each one. Muslims call a full reading a khatm, a sealing. This year is a long, slow khatm.
screen: `QUR'AN: A RECITATION, READ ALOUD` · `NOT THE ORDER IT CAME DOWN` · `FROM THE OPENING, ONWARD` · `A KHATM: A FULL READING, SEALED`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose a daily reading time. Not a big one. A slot that already exists in your day: after the dawn prayer, on the bus, with the first coffee, before you sleep. Sit now, and picture tomorrow. Where are you when you have five quiet minutes? Picture yourself there, opening the book or this app at that time. Let it become an appointment you keep. If you pray, you can say bismillah as you decide. The bell holds the time.
Khatm. A sealing — the name for a full reading of the Qur'an, which this year will be, a long, slow one. Today's word.
Your line: from the opening, onward. Today, set an alarm or a note for the reading time you chose, and keep it tomorrow. Day three hundred thirty-two.

screen: `DAY 332 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: SEVEN VERSES, SAID SEVENTEEN TIMES A DAY.`

333.title: Seven verses, said seventeen times a day
333.hook: the Fatiha is recited in every unit of every prayer
333.howItsDone: Muslims recite al-Fatiha standing in every rak'ah of every prayer, seventeen times a day across the five obligatory prayers; in the Hanafi school a worshipper praying behind an imam listens silently while the imam recites.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the whole book, this year's khatm, and your line: from the opening, onward. Did you choose a reading time, and did it hold? Day three hundred thirty-three.

Do some arithmetic with a Muslim who prays all five daily prayers. Dawn has two units of prayer, called rak'ahs. Noon has four. Afternoon, four. Sunset, three. Night, four. Add them up: seventeen. And in every one of those seventeen units, standing, the same short surah is recited. Seventeen times a day, before any optional prayers are counted. Over a year, more than six thousand times, from the same seven verses. Today: seven verses.
screen: `TWO, FOUR, FOUR, THREE, FOUR.` → `SEVENTEEN UNITS A DAY.` → `THE SAME SURAH IN EACH.`

segments.voice: Last year you learned al-Fatiha a line at a time. This year we stand back and look at the whole surah, and at what happens to words when they're repeated. The rule comes from a hadith in Bukhari and Muslim: the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ said there is no prayer for the one who does not recite the Opening of the Book. So the Fatiha is the one surah that can't be left out. Schools of law differ on one detail. Many say every worshipper recites it in each unit. Hanafi scholars teach that when you pray behind an imam, you stand silent, and the imam's recitation counts for the whole row. Either way, it's said in every unit. The Qur'an itself seems to point to this. In Surah al-Hijr, God tells the Prophet He has given him seven of the oft-repeated verses, and the great Qur'an. Many commentators, following a hadith in Bukhari, say those seven are the Fatiha. Its Arabic nickname comes from there: as-sab' al-mathani, the seven oft-repeated. In the count printed in many copies today, the bismillah is the first of the seven; some scholars count differently and still arrive at seven. Now the question repetition raises. Doesn't anything said seventeen times a day go numb? Muslim teachers raise it themselves. Scholars warn against prayer that's only motion, and teachers tell students to slow down, to hear one line freshly each time. The repetition is the container. What's poured into it changes from one prayer to the next. The most repeated words, said by a tired person at dawn and a grieving one at night, are never quite said the same way twice.
screen: `NO PRAYER WITHOUT THE OPENING` · `THE SEVEN OFT-REPEATED (15:87)` · `DOESN'T REPETITION GO NUMB?` · `THE SAME WORDS, NEVER SAID THE SAME`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: count how many times you say it today. If you pray, keep a quiet tally, a finger pressed against your thumb after each unit, and notice which time was most awake. If you don't pray, count something else: how many times today you hear the opening line, Praise be to Allah, or say it in your head. Right now, say the seven verses once, slowly, aloud or silently, or just sit with the number seventeen. The bell holds the time.
Seven verses. Al-Fatiha, the seven oft-repeated, recited in every unit of every prayer: seventeen times a day in the obligatory prayers alone. Today's word.
Your line: the most repeated words. Today, pick one of the seventeen, or one moment if you don't pray, and say it as if for the first time. Day three hundred thirty-three.

334.title: A conversation
334.hook: a sacred hadith says Allah answers each line of the Fatiha as it is said (Muslim)
334.howItsDone: Many Muslims recite al-Fatiha slowly, pausing at the end of each verse; teachers often cite the hadith qudsi in Sahih Muslim, in which God answers each line, as the reason for the pause.

segments.voice: Yesterday: seven verses, said seventeen times a day. Your line was the most repeated words. Did you count, and which time felt most awake? Day three hundred thirty-four.

There's a kind of phone call where you talk and nobody answers. Voicemail. You say your piece into the quiet, hang up, and hope it lands. Prayer can sound like that from the outside: words going out, silence coming back. Sahih Muslim preserves a hadith that pictures the Fatiha very differently. In it, every line the worshipper says gets a reply, right then, before the next line starts. Not voicemail. A conversation. Today we listen to both sides of it.
screen: `WORDS INTO THE QUIET.` → `WHAT IF EVERY LINE GOT A REPLY?` → `BOTH SIDES OF THE FATIHA.`

segments.voice: This is a hadith qudsi, a sacred hadith: words the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ reported from God Himself, but which are not part of the Qur'an. It's in Sahih Muslim. God says: I have divided the prayer between Myself and My servant into two halves, and My servant will have what he asks. Then it walks through the surah. The servant says: praise be to Allah, Lord of the Worlds. And God says: My servant has praised Me. The servant says: the Beneficent, the Merciful. God says: My servant has extolled Me. The servant says: Owner of the Day of Judgment. God says: My servant has glorified Me. Then the hinge, the middle verse: Thee alone we worship, Thee alone we ask for help. And God says: this is between Me and My servant, and My servant will have what he asked. Then the last lines, show us the straight path, and God says: this is for My servant, and My servant will have what he asked. Notice the shape. The first half belongs to God: praise. The middle is shared. The last half belongs to the person: a request. And every line gets an answer. One detail stands out. In this hadith, the replies aren't promised for a perfect recitation; they're described as coming each time the line is said. That's why some teachers tell people to pause a breath after each verse. Not because the reply needs time. Because the one praying needs a moment to remember there is one. He answers each line.
screen: `A SACRED HADITH, IN SAHIH MUSLIM` · `MY SERVANT HAS PRAISED ME` · `THE MIDDLE VERSE IS SHARED` · `PAUSE: THERE IS A REPLY`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pause after each line. Say the Fatiha now, aloud or silently, in Arabic or in English. After each verse, stop for one breath. In that breath, you can recall the reply from the hadith: praised, extolled, glorified, between Me and My servant, for My servant. If you don't pray, simply listen to the gaps between the lines, and notice how different the words feel with space around them. The bell holds the time.
A conversation. The Fatiha as two voices: the worshipper speaks a line, and in the sacred hadith God answers it, half praise, half request, the middle shared. Today's word.
Your line: he answers each line. Today, in one prayer or one quiet minute, leave a breath of space after each verse. Day three hundred thirty-four.

335.title: Praise, then ask
335.hook: the Fatiha praises for four verses before it asks for anything (1:1–7)
335.howItsDone: Many Muslims open a du'a by praising Allah and sending blessings on the Prophet before making their request, following the order of al-Fatiha and the hadith of Fadalah ibn Ubayd.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a conversation, and your line: he answers each line. Did you leave a breath of space between the verses? Today, look at the order those lines come in. Day three hundred thirty-five.

A text arrives: can you lend me fifty dollars. No hello. No how are you. Just the ask. Nothing wrong with it, exactly, but it lands hard. Now a different text: I was thinking about you this morning, you were so good to me last month, and, I hate to ask, could you help me out. Same request. Different weight. The Fatiha is seven verses long, and for the first four of them it asks for nothing at all. Today: praise.
screen: `JUST THE ASK.` → `OR: HELLO, THANK YOU, THEN THE ASK.` → `FOUR VERSES BEFORE ANY REQUEST.`

segments.voice: Count the verses as day three hundred thirty-three did, with the bismillah first. One: in the name of Allah, the Beneficent, the Merciful. Two: praise be to Allah, Lord of the Worlds. Three: the Beneficent, the Merciful. Four: Owner of the Day of Judgment. Four verses, and every one of them is about who God is. Then verse five turns: Thee alone we worship, Thee alone we ask for help. And only in verses six and seven comes a request: show us the straight path. The book's opening surah carries an order inside it. A hadith makes that order explicit. Fadalah ibn Ubayd reported, in the collections of Abu Dawud and at-Tirmidhi, that the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ heard a man making a supplication in his prayer without praising God or sending blessings on the Prophet. He said: this man has rushed. Then he taught: when one of you prays, begin with the praise of your Lord, then send blessings on the Prophet, then ask for whatever you wish. So Muslim supplications are often taught in that shape: praise, blessing, then the need. Praise puts the one being addressed first, before the want. It also changes the asking. A request made after four verses about mercy, lordship and judgment comes out smaller and clearer. The straight path, in the Fatiha, isn't a demand. It's what you ask for after you've remembered whom you're asking. Praise first. Then ask for anything.
screen: `FOUR VERSES ABOUT WHO GOD IS` · `VERSE FIVE: THE TURN` · `THIS MAN HAS RUSHED` · `PRAISE, BLESSING, THEN THE NEED`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: praise before you ask today. Sit now, and think of one thing you want, something real, large or small. Hold it, but don't say it yet. First, for a few breaths, name what you're grateful for, or, if you pray, what you know of God: merciful, near, the Lord of the worlds. Let that settle. Then, only at the end, let the request come. Notice whether it sounds different when it finally arrives. The bell holds the time.
Praise. The Fatiha spends four verses on who God is before it asks for anything, and the hadith calls skipping that step rushing. Today's word.
Your line: praise first. Today, before you ask anyone for something, a colleague, a parent, God, start with one honest word of thanks. Day three hundred thirty-five.

336.title: No doubt in it
336.hook: a book for the mindful: those who believe in the unseen, pray, and give (2:2–3)
336.tomorrow: The one who lit a fire
336.howItsDone: Muslims speak of taqwa as the aim of worship itself: the Qur'an names it as the purpose of fasting, and many say bismillah before ordinary acts to bring God to mind as they begin.

segments.voice: Yesterday: praise, and your line, praise first. Did one request today come after a word of thanks? The Fatiha ended asking for a path. Today the next page answers. Day three hundred thirty-six.

The Fatiha's last request is show us the straight path. Turn one page. Surah al-Baqarah opens with three Arabic letters, alif, lam, mim, whose meaning, most scholars say, God alone knows. And then, as if answering the request just made, the second verse. In Pickthall's words: “This is the Scripture whereof there is no doubt, a guidance unto those who ward off (evil).” You asked for guidance. Here it is. But notice who it says the guidance is for. Today: taqwa.
screen: `SHOW US THE STRAIGHT PATH.` → `ALIF, LAM, MIM.` → `HERE IS THE GUIDANCE.`

segments.voice: Those who ward off evil. Pickthall's phrase translates one Arabic word: al-muttaqin, the people of taqwa. Taqwa comes from a root, w-q-y, meaning to guard, to shield yourself. It gets translated as fear of God, piety, God-consciousness, mindfulness. Each catches a piece. A story from the early commentaries, retold by Ibn Kathir, gives a picture. Umar asked the companion Ubayy ibn Ka'b what taqwa is. Ubayy asked him: have you ever walked a path full of thorns? Yes. And what did you do? I gathered up my clothes and watched every step. That, said Ubayy, is taqwa. Not terror. Attention. Then verse three says what these mindful people look like: they believe in the unseen, they establish the prayer, and they spend from what they've been given. Three things. Trust in what you can't see. A practice that keeps returning, five times a day. And open hands. Here's what stands out. The book says it's guidance for the mindful, not guidance that makes you mindful first and then guides you. Many commentators read it as a loop. A little attention lets you hear the book, and the book deepens the attention. Look back at this week. A whole book opened. Seven verses said seventeen times a day. A conversation where every line gets an answer. Praise before asking. All of it was about attention. Taqwa is the name for that attention, walking carefully through a thorny world with God in mind.
screen: `AL-MUTTAQIN: THOSE WHO GUARD THEMSELVES` · `WALKING A PATH OF THORNS` · `THE UNSEEN, THE PRAYER, OPEN HANDS` · `THIS WEEK WAS ABOUT ATTENTION`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do one thing mindfully. Pick something small that's right in front of you: a glass of water, standing up, putting on your shoes. Do it slowly, the way you'd walk a path with thorns. Notice the weight of the glass, the cold, the swallow. Then sit, and let the attention stay on your breath. If you pray, you can say bismillah before you begin. The bell holds the time.
Taqwa. Mindfulness of God; from a root meaning to guard yourself, like gathering your clothes on a thorny path. The Qur'an calls itself guidance for the people of taqwa. Today's word.
Your line: guidance for the mindful. Today, do one ordinary task as if the path had thorns, slowly and awake. Day three hundred thirty-six.
